title: World History to 1500
description: A survey of world history from the earliest humans through the eve of global contact around 1500. You will trace how farming, cities, and writing gave rise to the first civilizations, how classical empires and world religions spread across Afro-Eurasia, and how distinct but connected civilizations flourished in medieval Asia, Africa, and the Americas.
outcomes: You can explain how the Neolithic Revolution led to the first cities and civilizations in Mesopotamia and Egypt.
You can describe the political and cultural achievements of classical Greece, Rome, India, and China.
You can trace how Christianity and Islam spread and shaped politics, law, and daily life across late antiquity.
You can explain how feudalism, the Islamic Golden Age, and the Crusades shaped the medieval Mediterranean world.
You can describe major medieval civilizations in East Asia, the Mongol Empire, and the kingdoms of sub-Saharan Africa.
You can describe the achievements of civilizations in the Americas and explain how the world's regions were connected by 1500.

units.title: The Ancient Near East and Egypt
units.summary: Farming allowed humans to settle permanently for the first time, and along two great river systems those settlements grew into the world's first cities, laws, and writing systems.

lessons.title: Human Origins and the Agricultural Revolution
lessons.intro: For nearly all of human history, every person on Earth survived by hunting animals and gathering wild plants, moving constantly in small bands, and then, within just a few thousand years, most humans switched to farming and never moved the same way again.

sections.heading: From Foraging to Farming
body: Modern humans, *Homo sapiens*, evolved in Africa roughly 300,000 years ago and gradually migrated across the globe, reaching every inhabited continent by around 15,000 years ago. For most of this **Paleolithic** period, people lived in small, mobile groups of hunter-gatherers, following seasonal food sources and leaving little permanent trace beyond stone tools and cave art.

Around 10,000 BCE, in a shift historians call the **Neolithic Revolution**, people in the **Fertile Crescent**, a region arcing through the Middle East, began deliberately planting crops like wheat and barley and domesticating animals like sheep and goats. Farming produced more reliable, storable food than foraging, which allowed populations to grow and, crucially, allowed some people to stop producing their own food entirely.

sections.heading: The Birth of Cities and Civilization
body: Farming's food surplus meant that not everyone needed to farm, freeing some people to become priests, soldiers, craftspeople, or rulers, a process historians call specialization. Early towns like Jericho and Çatalhöyük grew into some of the world's first permanent settlements, with populations in the thousands well before written history began.

Historians generally define a **civilization** by a cluster of features that tend to appear together: cities, organized government, a shared religion or belief system, job specialization, distinct social classes, and, most importantly for historians, writing, since writing is what allows a society's own voice to survive into the historical record. Mesopotamia and Egypt would be the first regions to develop all of these features together.

keyTerms.def: The long era of human history before farming, characterized by hunting, gathering, and small mobile groups.
The shift beginning around 10,000 BCE from foraging to farming and permanent settlement.
A crescent-shaped region in the Middle East where some of the earliest farming and civilizations developed.
A society marked by cities, organized government, religion, job specialization, social classes, and writing.

practice.q: What made the Neolithic Revolution a turning point in human history?
choices: It marked the first use of stone tools
It marked the shift from foraging to farming, enabling permanent settlement and population growth
It ended all warfare between human groups
It began human migration out of Africa
practice.explain: The Neolithic Revolution refers to humanity's shift from a mobile hunter-gatherer lifestyle to settled farming, which produced reliable food surpluses that allowed populations to grow and some people to specialize in non-farming work.

practice.q: Why is writing considered especially important among the traits historians use to define civilization?
choices: Writing is the only trait that appeared before farming
Writing allows a society to leave its own record for historians to study directly
Writing was invented before cities existed
Writing is not actually one of the traits historians use
practice.explain: While cities, government, and social classes can sometimes be inferred from physical remains, writing lets historians read a society's own words, laws, and stories directly, which is why it holds special importance in defining civilization.

practice.q: What allowed some members of early farming societies to become priests, soldiers, or craftspeople instead of food producers?
choices: The invention of the wheel
A reliable food surplus produced by farming, which meant not everyone needed to grow their own food
The domestication of horses
The development of writing
practice.explain: Farming produced more food than foragers typically gathered, and that surplus could support people who did not farm at all, enabling the job specialization that is a hallmark of early civilizations.

lessons.title: Mesopotamia: Cities, Law, and Empire
lessons.intro: Between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, in a land the Greeks later named Mesopotamia, competing city-states invented writing, built the world's first law codes, and repeatedly rose and fell as empires stretched across the region.

sections.heading: Sumer and the First Cities
body: By roughly 3500 BCE, the region of Sumer in southern Mesopotamia held some of the world's first true cities, including Uruk and Ur, each governed as an independent **city-state** with its own ruler and patron god. To track trade, taxes, and temple offerings, Sumerians developed **cuneiform**, a system of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay tablets, which became the world's earliest known writing system.

Sumerian religion was polytheistic, worshipping many gods tied to natural forces like storms and rivers, and each city built a massive stepped temple called a **ziggurat** at its center, symbolizing the connection between the city and its patron deity. Sumerian city-states frequently warred with one another over land and water rights, a pattern of rivalry that would eventually invite conquest by outside powers.

sections.heading: Empires of Mesopotamia
body: Around 2334 BCE, Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian city-states and built what historians consider the world's first empire, unifying multiple city-states and peoples under one ruler. Centuries later, the Babylonian king Hammurabi issued the **Code of Hammurabi** around 1754 BCE, one of the earliest and most complete surviving law codes, inscribed on a stone pillar for all to see.

Mesopotamian power later shifted to the Assyrians, whose large, disciplined armies and iron weapons built a brutal but effective empire, and finally to the Neo-Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar II, who rebuilt Babylon into a magnificent capital before the region fell to the Persian Empire in 539 BCE, ending nearly three thousand years of Mesopotamian political independence.

example.problem: The Code of Hammurabi punished the same crime differently depending on the social class of the victim and offender, for example imposing harsher penalties for harming a noble than for harming a commoner. What does this tell historians about Babylonian society?
steps: The code's class-based punishments show that Babylonian law did not treat all people as legally equal.
Society was organized into a clear hierarchy, at minimum nobles, commoners, and enslaved people, and the law explicitly protected higher-status individuals more strongly.

This tells historians that ancient legal codes often reinforced, rather than challenged, existing social inequality, even while introducing the important principle of publicly written, predictable law.
example.answer: The code's differing punishments by social class reveal that Babylonian society was strictly hierarchical, and that its famous written law reinforced, rather than eliminated, class-based inequality even as it introduced predictable, public legal standards.

keyTerms.def: The world's earliest known writing system, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay tablets by the Sumerians.
A massive stepped temple built at the center of Sumerian and later Mesopotamian cities.
A Babylonian law code from around 1754 BCE, among the earliest and most complete surviving written legal codes.
An independent political unit consisting of a city and its surrounding territory, common in early Sumer.

practice.q: What was cuneiform?
choices: A Mesopotamian irrigation system
The world's earliest known writing system, made of wedge-shaped marks on clay tablets
A Babylonian law code
A type of Sumerian temple
practice.explain: Cuneiform, developed by the Sumerians to record trade, taxes, and temple business, is recognized as the world's earliest known system of writing.

practice.q: The Code of Hammurabi is historically significant mainly because it
choices: Was the first religious text in Mesopotamia
Was one of the earliest and most complete surviving written law codes, publicly displayed
Abolished social class distinctions in Babylon
Established Sumerian city-states
practice.explain: The Code of Hammurabi, inscribed publicly around 1754 BCE, is significant as one of the earliest and most complete written legal codes to survive, revealing how Babylonian law was organized and enforced.

practice.q: Who is credited with building the world's first empire by unifying the Sumerian city-states?
choices: Hammurabi
Sargon of Akkad
Nebuchadnezzar II
Narmer
practice.explain: Sargon of Akkad conquered the independent Sumerian city-states around 2334 BCE and unified them under his rule, an achievement historians recognize as the world's first empire.

lessons.title: Ancient Egypt and the Nile
lessons.intro: While Mesopotamian city-states fought endlessly among themselves, Egypt's unique geography helped unify an entire river valley into one of history's longest-lasting civilizations, ruled by god-kings who built monuments meant to outlast time itself.

sections.heading: The Gift of the Nile
body: Egypt's civilization depended entirely on the **Nile River**, whose predictable annual flooding deposited rich, fertile silt along its banks, allowing reliable farming in an otherwise desert landscape; the Greek historian Herodotus later called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile.' Around 3100 BCE, a ruler traditionally identified as Narmer united Upper and Lower Egypt into a single kingdom, beginning a pattern of centralized rule that would last, with interruptions, for nearly three thousand years.

Egyptian kings, called **pharaohs**, were considered living gods responsible for maintaining *ma'at*, a divine cosmic order and balance. Egyptian history is traditionally divided into the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms, separated by periods of instability, with the Old Kingdom, roughly 2686 to 2181 BCE, producing the era's most famous monuments.

sections.heading: Egyptian Religion, Writing, and Legacy
body: Egyptian religion was richly polytheistic, and a strong belief in the afterlife shaped much of Egyptian culture: bodies were preserved through mummification and buried with belongings meant for use in the next life. The Old Kingdom's massive pyramids, especially at Giza, served as tombs and monuments to the pharaoh's divine power, requiring enormous organized labor and engineering skill.

Egyptians recorded their history and religion using **hieroglyphics**, a complex writing system combining pictures and phonetic symbols. Notable rulers include Hatshepsut, one of the few women to rule as pharaoh in her own right, who expanded trade networks, and Ramesses II, whose long reign and extensive building projects marked the height of New Kingdom power.

keyTerms.def: The title of ancient Egypt's ruler, regarded as a living god responsible for maintaining cosmic order.
Ancient Egypt's writing system, combining pictorial and phonetic symbols.
The river whose predictable annual flooding made farming possible and unified ancient Egyptian civilization.
The period of ancient Egyptian history, roughly 2686-2181 BCE, that produced the Giza pyramids.

practice.q: Why was the Nile River so essential to ancient Egyptian civilization?
choices: It provided a reliable trade route to Mesopotamia only
Its predictable annual flooding deposited fertile silt, enabling reliable farming in an otherwise desert region
It was the primary source of building stone for the pyramids
It separated Upper and Lower Egypt permanently
practice.explain: The Nile's predictable yearly flooding deposited nutrient-rich silt along its banks, making farming reliable in a landscape that would otherwise be desert, and this reliability underpinned Egypt's stability and prosperity.

practice.q: Egyptian pharaohs were regarded as
choices: Elected representatives of the people
Living gods responsible for maintaining divine cosmic order
Temporary military leaders only
Priests without political authority
practice.explain: Pharaohs held a unique religious status as living gods whose central duty was maintaining ma'at, the cosmic order and balance believed to sustain Egyptian society.

practice.q: The pyramids at Giza were built primarily as
choices: Granaries for storing surplus grain
Tombs and monuments to a pharaoh's divine power
Fortresses to defend against invasion
Temples dedicated to foreign gods
practice.explain: The Old Kingdom's great pyramids served as elaborate tombs and monuments meant to secure and display the pharaoh's divine power for eternity, requiring immense organized labor to construct.

units.title: Classical Civilizations
units.summary: Between roughly 800 BCE and 500 CE, Greece, Rome, India, and China each built political systems, philosophies, and empires whose ideas and institutions would influence the world for millennia afterward.

lessons.title: The Greek World
lessons.intro: Ancient Greece was never a single unified country but a scattering of fiercely independent city-states, and out of that very fragmentation and rivalry came experiments in government, especially in one city, that changed how humans think about power.

sections.heading: From Minoans to Poleis
body: Greek civilization's roots trace to the Bronze Age Minoan civilization on Crete and the Mycenaean civilization on the mainland, both of which collapsed around 1200 BCE, ushering in a poorly documented 'Dark Age.' Out of this period emerged the **polis**, or city-state, the fundamental Greek political unit, each fiercely independent and often at war with its neighbors.

Athens developed the world's first **democracy**, in which free adult male citizens voted directly on laws and policy, a system expanded under the statesman Pericles in the 400s BCE, though it excluded women, enslaved people, and foreigners from participation. Sparta, by contrast, built a militarized, oligarchic society organized almost entirely around producing disciplined soldiers, relying on a large enslaved population called helots to sustain its economy.

sections.heading: Golden Age, Conquest, and Legacy
body: Greek city-states briefly united to repel Persian invasions in the early 400s BCE, with Athenian-led forces winning a famous victory at Marathon in 490 BCE, but unity did not last. Athens and Sparta later fought each other directly in the devastating Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE), which ended in Spartan victory but left all of Greece weakened.

That weakness allowed Philip II of Macedon to conquer the Greek city-states, and his son **Alexander the Great** then conquered an empire stretching from Greece to Egypt and into India between 336 and 323 BCE. Alexander's conquests spread Greek language, art, and ideas across this vast territory, creating a blended **Hellenistic** culture that mixed Greek and local traditions long after his empire fragmented following his death.

keyTerms.def: An independent Greek city-state, the fundamental political unit of ancient Greece.
A system in ancient Athens in which free adult male citizens voted directly on laws and policy.
A devastating war (431-404 BCE) between Athens and Sparta that weakened all of Greece.
The blended Greek and local culture that spread across Alexander the Great's former empire after 323 BCE.

practice.q: Athenian democracy allowed direct political participation by
choices: All residents of Athens equally
Only free adult male citizens
Only wealthy landowners regardless of citizenship
Women and enslaved people exclusively
practice.explain: Athenian democracy was limited to free adult male citizens, excluding women, enslaved people, and foreign residents from voting and holding office, even as it pioneered direct citizen participation in government.

practice.q: What was the main long-term effect of Alexander the Great's conquests?
choices: The permanent unification of Greece under one government
The spread of a blended Hellenistic culture combining Greek and local traditions across a vast territory
The destruction of all Greek city-states
The founding of the Roman Republic
practice.explain: Alexander's rapid conquests spread Greek language, art, and institutions across his empire, and after his death that influence blended with local cultures into a lasting Hellenistic civilization stretching from Greece to Egypt and Central Asia.

practice.q: The Peloponnesian War was fought primarily between
choices: Greece and the Persian Empire
Athens and Sparta
Alexander the Great and Persia
Macedon and Egypt
practice.explain: The Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE) pitted Athens against Sparta in a prolonged, destructive conflict that ended in Spartan victory but weakened the entire Greek world.

lessons.title: Rome: Republic to Empire
lessons.intro: Rome began as a small city on the Italian peninsula ruled by kings, transformed itself into a republic governed by elected officials and a powerful Senate, and eventually became an empire spanning three continents before its western half collapsed.

sections.heading: The Roman Republic
body: According to tradition, Rome expelled its last king in 509 BCE and established the **Roman Republic**, a system in which elected officials called consuls led the government alongside an aristocratic Senate, balancing power to prevent any single person from ruling as a tyrant. Rome gradually expanded to control the entire Italian peninsula through military conquest and by extending citizenship to some conquered peoples.

Rome's greatest early test came in the **Punic Wars** (264-146 BCE) against Carthage, a powerful trading city in North Africa. In the Second Punic War, the Carthaginian general Hannibal famously marched an army, including war elephants, across the Alps into Italy and won stunning victories, yet Rome ultimately recovered and destroyed Carthage entirely by the war's end, becoming the dominant power in the western Mediterranean.

sections.heading: From Republic to Empire
body: Continued expansion strained the Republic's institutions, and ambitious generals like Julius Caesar built personal power bases that the Senate could not control. After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE and another round of civil war, his adopted heir Octavian emerged victorious and took the title **Augustus** in 27 BCE, becoming Rome's first emperor and ending the Republic in all but name.

Augustus ushered in the **Pax Romana**, roughly two centuries of relative peace and stability that allowed trade, law, and infrastructure like roads and aqueducts to flourish across the empire. The Western Roman Empire eventually collapsed in 476 CE, worn down by a combination of economic decline, political instability, overextended borders, and repeated invasions by Germanic peoples.

example.problem: Rome's fall in the west is usually explained by a single cause, like 'barbarian invasions,' but historians generally treat it as the result of several compounding problems. What were the main contributing factors?
steps: Economic strain: heavy taxation, inflation, and reliance on slave labor weakened the tax base and economic productivity over centuries.
Political instability: frequent civil wars and rapid turnover of emperors, especially in the third century CE, undermined effective governance.
Military pressure: the empire's long borders became harder to defend, and repeated invasions by Germanic groups eventually overwhelmed Roman defenses in the west.
example.answer: Rome's fall resulted from compounding economic strain, political instability from frequent civil wars, and military pressure from Germanic invasions along an overextended border, not any single cause acting alone.

keyTerms.def: Rome's system of government from 509 BCE, led by elected consuls and the Senate, before Augustus became emperor.
A series of wars (264-146 BCE) between Rome and Carthage that made Rome the dominant power in the western Mediterranean.
A roughly two-century period of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire beginning under Augustus.
The title taken by Octavian in 27 BCE, becoming Rome's first emperor and ending the Republic.

practice.q: The Roman Republic's system of government was designed to
choices: Give absolute power to a single hereditary king
Balance power between elected consuls and the Senate to prevent any one person ruling as a tyrant
Eliminate all forms of citizen participation
Rule only through military generals
practice.explain: The Republic, established after Rome expelled its last king, deliberately balanced power between elected consuls and the aristocratic Senate to prevent the concentration of power in a single ruler.

practice.q: Hannibal is best known for
choices: Founding the Roman Republic
Leading a Carthaginian army, including elephants, across the Alps into Italy during the Second Punic War
Becoming Rome's first emperor
Ending the Pax Romana
practice.explain: Hannibal's audacious march across the Alps and early victories in Italy made him one of history's most famous military commanders, even though Carthage ultimately lost the war to Rome.

practice.q: Which factor is NOT typically cited as a cause of the Western Roman Empire's fall?
choices: Economic strain and heavy taxation
Political instability and frequent civil wars
Repeated invasions by Germanic peoples
The founding of the Roman Republic in 509 BCE
practice.explain: The founding of the Republic in 509 BCE occurred nearly a thousand years before Rome's fall and is a starting point of Roman history, not a cause of its later collapse, unlike economic, political, and military pressures.

lessons.title: Classical India and China
lessons.intro: While Greece and Rome built their classical civilizations around the Mediterranean, powerful empires and enduring philosophies were also taking shape across South and East Asia, laying foundations that would outlast any single dynasty.

sections.heading: Empires and Ideas in India
body: The **Maurya Empire** unified much of the Indian subcontinent by around 320 BCE, reaching its height under Emperor Ashoka, who after a famously bloody conquest converted to Buddhism and thereafter promoted nonviolence, religious tolerance, and public works throughout his realm, inscribing his edicts on pillars across the empire. Buddhism, which originated with Siddhartha Gautama around the 5th century BCE, spread widely under Ashoka's patronage.

Centuries later, the **Gupta Empire** (roughly 320-550 CE) presided over what is often called a golden age of Indian civilization, producing major achievements in mathematics, including the concept of zero as a number and the numeral system later transmitted to the Islamic world and Europe, as well as advances in astronomy, medicine, and Sanskrit literature.

sections.heading: Dynasties and Philosophy in China
body: In 221 BCE, the ruler known as Shi Huangdi unified competing warring states under the short-lived but transformative **Qin Dynasty**, standardizing writing, currency, and measurements across China and beginning construction connecting earlier defensive walls into what became the Great Wall. Though the Qin Dynasty collapsed quickly after his death, its centralizing reforms outlasted it.

The following Han Dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE) adopted **Confucianism**, a philosophy emphasizing social harmony, respect for hierarchy and elders, and ethical governance, as the basis for its civil administration, a choice that would shape Chinese government for two thousand years. The Han also opened the **Silk Road**, a network of trade routes connecting China to Central Asia, India, and eventually the Roman world, exchanging silk, spices, and ideas across Eurasia.

keyTerms.def: An empire that unified much of India around 320 BCE, reaching its height under the Buddhist emperor Ashoka.
An Indian empire (roughly 320-550 CE) known as a golden age of mathematics, science, and literature.
The dynasty that unified China in 221 BCE under Shi Huangdi and standardized writing, currency, and measurements.
A network of trade routes connecting China to Central Asia, India, and the Mediterranean world.

practice.q: Emperor Ashoka of the Maurya Empire is best known for
choices: Conquering all of China
Converting to Buddhism after a bloody conquest and thereafter promoting nonviolence and tolerance
Founding the Gupta Empire
Inventing the concept of zero
practice.explain: Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism following a violent conquest led him to promote nonviolence, religious tolerance, and public works, spreading Buddhism widely through inscribed edicts across his empire.

practice.q: The Gupta Empire is especially remembered for its contributions to
choices: Military conquest of the Roman Empire
Mathematics, including the concept of zero, along with advances in astronomy and medicine
The invention of Confucianism
The construction of the Great Wall
practice.explain: The Gupta Empire's golden age produced major mathematical advances, including treating zero as a number, along with significant progress in astronomy, medicine, and literature.

practice.q: Confucianism, adopted as a basis for Han Dynasty government, emphasized
choices: Individual liberty above social duty
Social harmony, respect for hierarchy, and ethical governance
Rejection of all government authority
Military conquest as the highest virtue
practice.explain: Confucianism stressed social harmony, respect for established hierarchy and elders, and ethical conduct in governance, and the Han Dynasty adopted it as the philosophical basis for its civil administration.

units.title: Religions and Empires of Late Antiquity
units.summary: As the Roman Empire weakened and eventually split, two new monotheistic faiths, Christianity and Islam, rose from small movements to reshape the political and cultural map of Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa.

lessons.title: The Rise of Christianity
lessons.intro: Christianity began as a small, persecuted Jewish sect in a remote Roman province and, within four centuries, became the official religion of the empire that had once tried to crush it.

sections.heading: From Persecuted Sect to State Religion
body: Jesus of Nazareth taught and was executed by Roman authorities in Judea around 30 CE, and his followers, believing he had risen from the dead, began spreading his teachings across the Roman world. The apostle Paul's extensive missionary journeys were especially important in spreading Christianity beyond its Jewish origins to Gentile, non-Jewish, communities throughout the Mediterranean.

Roman authorities periodically persecuted Christians for refusing to worship the emperor or Roman gods, but the faith kept spreading despite this pressure. In 313 CE, the emperor Constantine issued the **Edict of Milan**, granting religious tolerance to Christians, and he personally converted, dramatically changing Christianity's fortunes; by 380 CE it had become the empire's official religion.

sections.heading: Doctrine, Councils, and Division
body: As Christianity grew, disputes arose over core doctrine, particularly the nature of Jesus and his relationship to God. Constantine convened the **Council of Nicaea** in 325 CE to resolve these disputes, producing the Nicene Creed, a statement of core Christian belief still recited in many churches today, and establishing a pattern of church councils settling doctrinal disagreements.

Over subsequent centuries, the eastern and western branches of the church, centered respectively in Constantinople and Rome, grew apart over language, doctrine, and authority, particularly disputes over the pope's authority. This division became formal in the **Great Schism** of 1054, splitting Christianity into the Roman Catholic Church in the west and the Eastern Orthodox Church in the east.

keyTerms.def: A 313 CE decree by Emperor Constantine granting religious tolerance to Christians in the Roman Empire.
A 325 CE church council convened by Constantine that produced the Nicene Creed and settled early doctrinal disputes.
The 1054 split between the Roman Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church.
The office and authority of the pope, the bishop of Rome, as head of the Roman Catholic Church.

practice.q: The Edict of Milan in 313 CE
choices: Made Christianity the empire's only legal religion
Granted religious tolerance to Christians within the Roman Empire
Split Christianity into Catholic and Orthodox branches
Executed Jesus of Nazareth
practice.explain: The Edict of Milan, issued by Constantine, granted religious tolerance to Christians, ending official persecution, though it took until 380 CE for Christianity to become the empire's official religion.

practice.q: What caused the Great Schism of 1054?
choices: A dispute over whether Jesus existed
Growing division between the eastern and western churches over language, doctrine, and papal authority
The Council of Nicaea's decisions
Constantine's conversion to Christianity
practice.explain: Centuries of growing separation between the Rome-centered western church and the Constantinople-centered eastern church, especially over the pope's authority, culminated in the formal split of 1054.

practice.q: The Council of Nicaea in 325 CE was convened primarily to
choices: Elect the first pope
Resolve doctrinal disputes about the nature of Jesus and produce a shared statement of belief
Declare war on Rome's enemies
End the persecution of Christians
practice.explain: Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea specifically to settle theological disputes within the growing Christian church, resulting in the Nicene Creed as a shared statement of core belief.

lessons.title: The Rise of Islam
lessons.intro: Within a single century of its founding, Islam spread from a single city in the Arabian desert to control territory stretching from Spain to the borders of India, one of the fastest expansions of any religion or empire in world history.

sections.heading: Muhammad and the Origins of Islam
body: Muhammad, born in Mecca around 570 CE, began receiving what Muslims believe were divine revelations around 610 CE, which were later compiled into the **Quran**, Islam's holy book. Facing opposition and persecution in Mecca, Muhammad and his followers migrated to Medina in 622 CE in an event called the **Hijra**, which marks year one of the Islamic calendar.

Islam's core practices are organized around the **Five Pillars**: declaring faith in one God with Muhammad as his prophet, praying five times daily, giving to charity, fasting during the month of Ramadan, and making a pilgrimage to Mecca if able. By the time of Muhammad's death in 632 CE, Islam had united much of the Arabian Peninsula under a single faith and community.

sections.heading: The Spread of the Islamic Empire
body: After Muhammad's death, a dispute arose over who should lead the Muslim community, a disagreement that eventually produced a lasting split between **Sunni** Muslims, who accepted elected successors called caliphs, and **Shia** Muslims, who believed leadership should stay within Muhammad's family line through his cousin Ali. Despite this division, the early caliphates expanded with astonishing speed, conquering Persia, much of the Byzantine Middle East and North Africa, and Spain within about a century.

The Abbasid Caliphate, which came to power in 750 CE, moved the capital to Baghdad, which grew into one of the world's great centers of trade, science, and learning, overseeing what historians call the Islamic Golden Age of scholarship that preserved and expanded on Greek, Persian, and Indian knowledge.

example.problem: After Muhammad's death in 632 CE with no named successor, a dispute over leadership eventually split Islam into Sunni and Shia branches. What was the core disagreement?
steps: One group believed the community should choose its own leader, a caliph, based on ability and consensus among the Muslim community, regardless of family lineage.
The other group believed leadership should have passed specifically to Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, Ali, and remained within Muhammad's family line.
This disagreement over legitimate succession, not a difference in core theology, is the historical root of the Sunni-Shia division that persists today.
example.answer: The split originated in a disagreement over succession: Sunnis accepted elected caliphs chosen by the community, while Shia Muslims believed leadership belonged within Muhammad's family, specifically to his cousin Ali.

keyTerms.def: The five core practices of Islam: faith, prayer, charity, fasting, and pilgrimage to Mecca.
Muhammad's 622 CE migration from Mecca to Medina, marking year one of the Islamic calendar.
An Islamic state led by a caliph, considered a political and religious successor to Muhammad.
The two main branches of Islam, divided originally over the question of rightful succession after Muhammad's death.

practice.q: What event does the Hijra refer to, and why is it significant?
choices: Muhammad's birth in Mecca, marking the start of Islam
Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, which marks year one of the Islamic calendar
The conquest of Baghdad by the Abbasids
The composition of the Quran
practice.explain: The Hijra was Muhammad's 622 CE migration from Mecca to Medina after facing persecution, and it is significant enough to mark the starting point of the Islamic calendar.

practice.q: The Sunni-Shia split within Islam originated primarily from a disagreement over
choices: The content of the Quran
Who should legitimately lead the Muslim community after Muhammad's death
Whether to expand the Islamic empire
The location of the Hijra
practice.explain: The division arose from a dispute over succession: whether leadership should go to an elected caliph chosen by the community (Sunni view) or remain within Muhammad's family line through Ali (Shia view).

practice.q: Under the Abbasid Caliphate, Baghdad became known especially for
choices: Being the first Muslim city ever founded
Serving as a great center of trade, science, and learning during the Islamic Golden Age
Rejecting all foreign knowledge
Being conquered by the Byzantine Empire
practice.explain: After the Abbasids moved the capital to Baghdad in 750 CE, the city flourished as a center of trade and scholarship, overseeing an Islamic Golden Age that preserved and built upon Greek, Persian, and Indian knowledge.

lessons.title: Byzantium and the Fall of Rome in the West
lessons.intro: While the western half of the Roman Empire collapsed under waves of invasion in the fifth century, its eastern half survived for another thousand years, preserving Roman law and Greek learning under a new name: Byzantium.

sections.heading: The Western Empire Falls
body: By the late 300s CE, the Western Roman Empire faced mounting pressure from Germanic peoples migrating westward, themselves partly pushed by the Huns advancing from Central Asia. In 410 CE, the Visigoths, led by Alaric, shocked the ancient world by sacking Rome itself, a city that had not fallen to a foreign enemy in eight centuries.

The western empire limped on for several more decades amid economic decline and repeated invasions, until in 476 CE the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, an event historians traditionally mark as the fall of the Western Roman Empire, even though many Roman institutions and traditions persisted locally afterward in modified form.

sections.heading: The Byzantine Empire Endures
body: The eastern half of the empire, centered on **Constantinople**, survived and thrived long after Rome's western collapse, becoming what historians call the Byzantine Empire. Emperor Justinian, who ruled from 527 to 565 CE, compiled **Justinian's Code**, a systematic organization of Roman law that would later influence legal systems across Europe, and he built the magnificent domed church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.

Byzantine scholars and monks preserved and copied classical Greek and Roman texts throughout the medieval period, texts that might otherwise have been lost, and this preserved knowledge later helped fuel the European Renaissance. The Byzantine Empire finally fell in 1453 CE, when Ottoman Turkish forces captured Constantinople, ending the last direct political continuation of the Roman Empire.

keyTerms.def: The capital of the Byzantine Empire, the eastern continuation of the Roman Empire, until its fall in 1453.
A systematic compilation of Roman law completed under Emperor Justinian in the 6th century CE.
The great domed church built in Constantinople under Emperor Justinian.
The eastern continuation of the Roman Empire, which survived the west's fall by nearly a thousand years.

practice.q: What event in 476 CE is traditionally used to mark the fall of the Western Roman Empire?
choices: The sack of Rome by the Visigoths
Odoacer's deposing of the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus
The fall of Constantinople
The Council of Nicaea
practice.explain: Historians traditionally date the fall of the Western Roman Empire to 476 CE, when the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus.

practice.q: Justinian's Code is significant because it
choices: Established the Byzantine Empire's official religion
Systematically organized Roman law in a form that later influenced European legal systems
Ended the Byzantine Empire
Was written after the fall of Constantinople
practice.explain: Justinian's Code compiled and systematized centuries of Roman legal tradition, and this organized body of law went on to shape the development of legal systems across medieval and modern Europe.

practice.q: The Byzantine Empire finally fell in 1453 CE when
choices: The Visigoths sacked Constantinople
Ottoman Turkish forces captured Constantinople
Justinian died
The Great Schism occurred
practice.explain: The Byzantine Empire, the long-surviving eastern continuation of Rome, finally ended in 1453 CE when Ottoman Turkish forces captured its capital, Constantinople.

units.title: Medieval Europe and the Islamic World
units.summary: As Western Europe fragmented into a patchwork of feudal lordships bound together mainly by the Catholic Church, the neighboring Islamic world built centers of scholarship and trade, and two centuries of holy war connected, and divided, both civilizations.

lessons.title: Feudal Europe and the Catholic Church
lessons.intro: After Rome's fall left no strong central authority in Western Europe, a new political and social system emerged from the wreckage, one built not on citizenship or law codes but on personal bonds of loyalty between lords, vassals, and the land they controlled together.

sections.heading: The Structure of Feudal Society
body: Following the collapse of Charlemagne's briefly reunified empire in the 800s, Western Europe fragmented into competing regional powers with little central authority to provide protection or order. **Feudalism** emerged as a practical response: a king or great lord granted land to lesser lords, called vassals, in exchange for military service and loyalty, and those vassals could in turn grant portions of their own land to knights beneath them.

This system rested economically on **manorialism**, in which peasants called **serfs** worked the land of a manor in exchange for protection and a share of the harvest, though serfs were legally bound to the land and could not simply leave. Medieval society was often described as divided into three estates: those who prayed (clergy), those who fought (nobility), and those who worked (peasants).

sections.heading: The Power of the Medieval Church
body: With political authority so fragmented, the Catholic Church became Western Europe's most unifying institution, sharing a common Latin language, canon law, and religious practice across every kingdom. Monasteries preserved literacy and classical learning through the copying of manuscripts, serving as rare islands of education in an otherwise largely illiterate society.

The Church's authority sometimes clashed directly with kings and emperors over who had the right to appoint bishops, a conflict known as the **Investiture Controversy**, resolved by compromise in 1122. Such conflicts show that in medieval Europe, spiritual and political power were deeply intertwined, and disputes over one frequently became disputes over the other.

keyTerms.def: A medieval political system in which land was exchanged for military service and loyalty between lords and vassals.
The economic system in which peasants worked a lord's land in exchange for protection and a share of the harvest.
A peasant legally bound to work a lord's land under the manorial system.
A medieval conflict between popes and monarchs over the right to appoint bishops, resolved by compromise in 1122.

practice.q: Feudalism developed primarily as a response to
choices: The strength of the Catholic Church
The lack of strong central authority after Charlemagne's empire fragmented
The success of the Crusades
The fall of Constantinople
practice.explain: With no strong central government to provide protection after Charlemagne's empire broke apart, feudalism offered a practical, decentralized system of mutual obligation between lords and vassals to maintain order and defense.

practice.q: How did serfdom differ from simple wage labor?
choices: Serfs were paid a fixed wage for their work
Serfs were legally bound to the manor's land and could not freely leave
Serfs owned the land they worked
Serfs had no obligations to their lord
practice.explain: Unlike free wage laborers, serfs were legally tied to a specific manor's land, unable to leave without permission, in exchange for the lord's protection and a share of what they produced.

practice.q: The Investiture Controversy was a dispute over
choices: Who had the right to appoint bishops, kings or the pope
The location of the Catholic Church's headquarters
Whether serfs could own land
The legitimacy of feudalism
practice.explain: The Investiture Controversy centered on whether kings and emperors or the pope held the rightful authority to appoint church bishops, a conflict that revealed how entangled religious and political power were in medieval Europe.

lessons.title: The Islamic Golden Age
lessons.intro: While parts of medieval Europe struggled with fragmentation and limited literacy, cities across the Islamic world became thriving centers of scholarship, translating and expanding ancient knowledge in ways that would later reshape science and mathematics worldwide.

sections.heading: Centers of Learning
body: In Baghdad, the Abbasid Caliphate founded the **House of Wisdom**, a major center of translation and research where scholars translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts into Arabic and then expanded on them, preserving classical knowledge that was largely inaccessible in Western Europe at the time. This translation movement, spanning roughly the 8th through 10th centuries CE, laid the foundation for major advances across multiple fields.

The mathematician **al-Khwarizmi**, working in Baghdad in the 9th century, wrote foundational texts on algebra, a word derived from the Arabic term *al-jabr* used in his work, and helped popularize the Hindu-Arabic numeral system, including the use of zero, that eventually replaced Roman numerals across the world. In medicine, the scholar Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, wrote an influential medical encyclopedia used in European universities for centuries.

sections.heading: Trade and Culture Across the Islamic World
body: Islamic trade networks stretched from Spain to India, connecting the Mediterranean, the Silk Road, and Indian Ocean trade routes, and merchants carried not just goods like textiles and spices but also scientific and philosophical ideas across this vast expanse. Islamic Spain, known as **al-Andalus**, became a notable center where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars often worked and studied side by side, particularly in the city of Córdoba.

Islamic civilization also produced significant agricultural and architectural innovations, including advanced irrigation techniques that spread new crops across the Mediterranean world, and distinctive architectural styles, seen for example in the intricate geometric designs of mosques, that would influence building traditions well beyond the Islamic world.

keyTerms.def: A major center of translation and scholarship in Abbasid Baghdad that preserved and expanded classical knowledge.
A 9th-century Baghdad mathematician whose work founded algebra and helped popularize the Hindu-Arabic numeral system.
Islamic Spain, a region known for scholarly exchange among Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars.
A branch of mathematics whose name derives from the Arabic al-jabr, developed by scholars including al-Khwarizmi.

practice.q: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad is best described as
choices: A military fortress
A major center of translation and scholarship that preserved and expanded classical knowledge
A mosque built for religious ceremonies only
A trading post on the Silk Road
practice.explain: The House of Wisdom served as a hub where scholars translated Greek, Persian, and Indian texts into Arabic and built new knowledge on that foundation, becoming central to the Islamic Golden Age of scholarship.

practice.q: What is al-Khwarizmi's most significant lasting contribution?
choices: Founding the city of Baghdad
Foundational work in algebra and helping popularize the Hindu-Arabic numeral system, including zero
Translating the Quran into Latin
Building the Hagia Sophia
practice.explain: Al-Khwarizmi's 9th-century mathematical writings founded the field of algebra, whose name derives from his work, and he helped spread the Hindu-Arabic numeral system, including the use of zero, that remains standard worldwide today.

practice.q: Al-Andalus, or Islamic Spain, was notable for
choices: Banning all non-Muslim scholars
Serving as a center where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars often studied side by side
Being the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate
Rejecting classical Greek learning entirely
practice.explain: Al-Andalus, especially the city of Córdoba, became known as a place where scholars of different faiths often worked and studied together, contributing to a rich intellectual exchange in medicine, philosophy, and science.

lessons.title: The Crusades
lessons.intro: For two centuries, waves of European Christian armies marched east to seize the Holy Land from Muslim control, and the long, bloody conflict that followed reshaped politics, trade, and religious relations across three continents.

sections.heading: Holy War Begins
body: In 1095, **Pope Urban II** called for a military expedition to reclaim Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim control, promising spiritual rewards to those who took up the cross. Tens of thousands of knights, nobles, and commoners responded, motivated by a genuine mix of religious devotion, hope for land and plunder, and, for some rulers, a chance to extend papal and royal authority.

The **First Crusade** succeeded in capturing Jerusalem in 1099, establishing several small Crusader states along the eastern Mediterranean coast, though the brutal conduct of the crusading armies, including massacres of the city's inhabitants, left lasting bitterness among both Muslims and Jews in the region.

sections.heading: Consequences of Centuries of Conflict
body: Later Crusades largely failed to achieve their goals. The Muslim general **Saladin** famously recaptured Jerusalem in 1187, prompting further crusading efforts that ultimately could not reverse Muslim control of the region permanently. The Fourth Crusade in 1204 took a bizarre and destructive turn when crusading forces, diverted by political and financial pressures, sacked Constantinople, a Christian city, severely weakening the Byzantine Empire rather than fighting Muslim forces at all.

Despite their military failure to hold the Holy Land long-term, the Crusades had lasting effects: they increased trade and cultural contact between Europe and the Islamic world, exposing Europeans to Islamic scholarship, goods, and technology, even as they deepened religious hostility and left the weakened Byzantine Empire more vulnerable to eventual Ottoman conquest.

example.problem: Historians describe the motives behind the Crusades as a genuine mixture rather than a single, simple cause. What were the main motivating factors, and why does it matter that historians treat them as mixed?
steps: Religious motive: many crusaders sincerely believed reclaiming the Holy Land was a sacred duty and that participating could earn spiritual forgiveness.
Economic and political motive: younger sons without inheritance rights sought land and plunder abroad, while the papacy and some kings saw opportunities to expand their own authority and influence.

Treating the motives as mixed matters because it avoids oversimplifying a complex historical event into either pure religious zeal or pure greed, when in reality both forces operated together and reinforced each other.
example.answer: The Crusades were driven by a genuine mixture of religious devotion, hopes for land and plunder, and political ambition; recognizing this mixture, rather than reducing the Crusades to a single motive, gives a more accurate picture of why so many people from different backgrounds joined.

keyTerms.def: The pope who called for the First Crusade in 1095 to reclaim the Holy Land from Muslim control.
The 1096-1099 Crusade that succeeded in capturing Jerusalem and established Crusader states in the region.
The Muslim general who recaptured Jerusalem from Crusader control in 1187.
The 1204 Crusade that was diverted into sacking Constantinople, severely weakening the Byzantine Empire.

practice.q: What did Pope Urban II call for in 1095?
choices: The Council of Nicaea
A military expedition to reclaim Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim control
The Investiture Controversy compromise
An alliance with the Byzantine Empire against Rome
practice.explain: In 1095, Pope Urban II called on European Christians to take up arms and reclaim the Holy Land, launching what became known as the First Crusade.

practice.q: The Fourth Crusade in 1204 is notable because
choices: It successfully reclaimed Jerusalem permanently
Crusading forces were diverted into sacking Constantinople, a Christian city, weakening the Byzantine Empire
It was called off before it began
It united Christian and Muslim forces against a common enemy
practice.explain: Rather than fighting Muslim forces, the Fourth Crusade was diverted by political and financial pressures into attacking and sacking Constantinople in 1204, severely damaging the Byzantine Empire it was nominally meant to support.

practice.q: One lasting non-military effect of the Crusades was
choices: The permanent unification of Europe under one government
Increased trade and cultural contact between Europe and the Islamic world
The end of Christianity in Europe
The founding of the Ottoman Empire
practice.explain: Even though the Crusades ultimately failed to hold the Holy Land permanently, the sustained contact they created between Europeans and the Islamic world increased trade and exposed Europeans to Islamic science, goods, and scholarship.

units.title: Asia and Africa in the Middle Ages
units.summary: Far from Europe's fragmented feudal kingdoms, medieval China built sophisticated bureaucracies and technologies, the Mongols forged the largest land empire in history, and powerful trading kingdoms rose across sub-Saharan Africa.

lessons.title: Tang and Song China
lessons.intro: Between roughly 600 and 1300 CE, China experienced two of its most creative and prosperous dynasties, producing inventions and institutions, from gunpowder to a merit-based bureaucracy, that would influence the entire world.

sections.heading: The Tang Dynasty's Golden Age
body: After a period of division following the Han Dynasty's collapse, the **Tang Dynasty** (618-907 CE) reunified China and built a cosmopolitan empire centered on the capital Chang'an, then one of the largest and most diverse cities in the world, attracting merchants and travelers along the Silk Road. Buddhism, which had entered China centuries earlier from India, spread widely during this period, blending with existing Confucian and Daoist traditions.

Tang China also pioneered woodblock printing, allowing texts to be reproduced far more efficiently than by hand-copying, which supported the spread of literacy, religious texts, and administrative documents throughout the empire.

sections.heading: Song Innovation and Economy
body: The **Song Dynasty** (960-1279 CE) presided over what historians sometimes call a medieval economic revolution: agricultural improvements, especially fast-ripening rice varieties, supported rapid population growth, while advances in shipbuilding and paper currency encouraged extensive internal and maritime trade. Song China refined the **civil service examination** system, in which government positions were awarded based on rigorous testing of Confucian classics rather than noble birth alone, creating a relatively meritocratic path to political power.

The Song era also gave the world three transformative inventions: **gunpowder**, initially developed for fireworks and later adapted for weapons; the magnetic compass, which revolutionized navigation; and movable type printing, refining on the earlier woodblock method. Song society also saw the emergence of foot binding among elite women, a painful practice that would persist in China for centuries.

keyTerms.def: The Chinese dynasty (618-907 CE) that reunified China and built a cosmopolitan empire centered on Chang'an.
The Chinese dynasty (960-1279 CE) known for economic growth, meritocratic bureaucracy, and major inventions.
A testing system used to select government officials based on knowledge of Confucian classics rather than noble birth.
An explosive compound first developed in Song-era China, initially for fireworks and later adapted for weapons.

practice.q: The civil service examination system, refined under the Song Dynasty, selected government officials based on
choices: Noble birth alone
Rigorous testing of knowledge, especially of Confucian classics, rather than family status
Military rank
Wealth alone
practice.explain: The civil service examination system tested candidates on their knowledge of Confucian texts, creating a relatively meritocratic path to government office that did not depend solely on noble birth.

practice.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the major Song Dynasty innovations?
choices: Gunpowder
The magnetic compass
Movable type printing
The Code of Hammurabi
practice.explain: The Code of Hammurabi was a Babylonian law code from nearly two thousand years before the Song Dynasty, unrelated to Song China's inventions of gunpowder, the compass, and movable type printing.

practice.q: The Tang Dynasty's capital, Chang'an, was notable for being
choices: A small, isolated village
One of the largest and most cosmopolitan cities in the world at the time
Located far from any trade routes
Built after the Song Dynasty ended
practice.explain: Chang'an, the Tang capital, was a major cosmopolitan hub that attracted merchants and travelers from across the Silk Road, making it one of the largest and most diverse cities in the world during this era.

lessons.title: The Mongol Empire
lessons.intro: In little more than a generation, a single leader united fractious nomadic tribes on the Central Asian steppe and built the largest contiguous land empire the world has ever seen, one that both devastated and connected civilizations across Eurasia.

sections.heading: Genghis Khan and Conquest
body: In 1206, a Mongol leader took the title **Genghis Khan**, meaning 'universal ruler,' after uniting the fractious nomadic tribes of the Central Asian steppe under his authority. His highly mobile, disciplined cavalry armies then conquered an astonishing amount of territory, from northern China through Central Asia into Persia and parts of Eastern Europe, within just a few decades.

Mongol conquest was often extremely brutal, with cities that resisted facing massacre and destruction as a deliberate strategy to discourage further resistance elsewhere. At the same time, Mongol rule was known for effective administration once conquest was complete, including religious tolerance, promotion of trade, and reliance on skilled local administrators regardless of their ethnicity or faith.

sections.heading: The Pax Mongolica
body: After Genghis Khan's death, his empire divided among his descendants into several **khanates**, regional Mongol states, including the Golden Horde in Russia, the Ilkhanate in Persia, and the **Yuan Dynasty** in China, founded by his grandson Kublai Khan in 1271. Despite this political division, the Mongol Empire maintained relatively secure trade routes across its territories, a period historians call the *Pax Mongolica*, or Mongol Peace.

This unprecedented connectivity across Eurasia allowed increased Silk Road trade and cultural exchange, famously including the travels of the Venetian merchant Marco Polo through Mongol territories in the late 1200s. The same connectivity, however, also allowed the rapid spread of disease, and historians believe Mongol trade routes helped carry the Black Death from Asia into Europe in the mid-1300s.

keyTerms.def: The Mongol leader who united Central Asian tribes in 1206 and built the world's largest contiguous land empire.
One of the regional states into which the Mongol Empire divided after Genghis Khan's death.
The Mongol-ruled dynasty in China, founded in 1271 by Kublai Khan.
The period of relatively secure trade and travel across Mongol-controlled Eurasia, enabling increased cultural exchange.

practice.q: What allowed Genghis Khan to build such a vast empire so quickly?
choices: Advanced naval technology
Uniting the Mongol tribes and deploying highly mobile, disciplined cavalry armies
An alliance with the Byzantine Empire
The invention of gunpowder
practice.explain: Genghis Khan's success rested on uniting previously fractious Mongol tribes and organizing them into highly mobile, disciplined cavalry forces capable of rapid, coordinated conquest across vast distances.

practice.q: The Pax Mongolica refers to
choices: A permanent peace treaty ending all Mongol conquest
A period of relatively secure trade and travel across Mongol-controlled territory, enabling cultural exchange
The Mongol conquest of China
The division of the Mongol Empire into khanates
practice.explain: The Pax Mongolica describes the relative safety and connectivity of trade routes across the vast, Mongol-controlled Eurasian landmass, which enabled increased trade and cultural exchange, including Marco Polo's travels.

practice.q: What unintended consequence did the connectivity of the Pax Mongolica also enable?
choices: A permanent decline in Silk Road trade
The rapid spread of the Black Death from Asia into Europe
The founding of the Ottoman Empire
The fall of the Byzantine Empire
practice.explain: The same trade routes that connected Mongol territory and enabled cultural exchange also allowed disease to travel quickly, and historians believe these routes helped carry the Black Death into Europe in the mid-1300s.

lessons.title: Sub-Saharan African Kingdoms
lessons.intro: Across medieval West and East Africa, powerful kingdoms grew wealthy controlling trade in gold, salt, and other goods, building centers of Islamic learning and coastal trading cities that connected Africa directly to the wider Indian Ocean world.

sections.heading: Ghana and Mali: Empires of Gold and Salt
body: The **Ghana Empire**, flourishing roughly between 300 and 1200 CE in West Africa, grew wealthy by controlling and taxing the trans-Saharan trade routes that carried gold northward and salt southward across the desert, two commodities each region desperately needed from the other. Ghana's rulers converted to Islam through contact with North African traders, though much of the population retained traditional beliefs.

Ghana's power eventually passed to the **Mali Empire**, which controlled even more of the gold trade at its height in the 1300s. Mali's most famous ruler, **Mansa Musa**, undertook a legendary pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, traveling with an enormous retinue and reportedly distributing so much gold along the way that he temporarily disrupted regional gold prices, an episode that made Mali's wealth famous as far away as Europe.

example.problem: Historical accounts describe Mansa Musa distributing so much gold during his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca that it caused gold prices in parts of the region to fall for years afterward. What does this reveal about Mali's economic role in medieval world trade?
steps: A single ruler's personal spending having a measurable effect on regional gold prices shows that Mali controlled an enormous share of the era's gold supply.
This wealth stemmed from Mali's control over key trans-Saharan trade routes carrying gold north from West African goldfields.
The episode also shows how interconnected medieval economies already were, since a disruption originating in West Africa could affect markets across North Africa and the Mediterranean.
example.answer: The episode reveals that Mali controlled such a large share of the era's gold supply that one ruler's spending could shift regional prices, underscoring both Mali's economic dominance and how interconnected medieval trade networks already were.

sections.heading: Songhai and the East African Coast
body: Mali eventually declined and was succeeded by the **Songhai Empire**, which by the 1400s and 1500s controlled an even larger territory along the Niger River. Under Songhai rule, the city of **Timbuktu** flourished as a renowned center of Islamic scholarship, home to a large library and a university that attracted scholars from across the Muslim world.

Along Africa's eastern coast, an entirely separate trading world developed among **Swahili** city-states such as Kilwa, Mombasa, and Zanzibar, which grew wealthy trading gold, ivory, and enslaved people with merchants across the Indian Ocean, reaching as far as Arabia, India, and China. These coastal cities blended African, Arab, and Persian cultural influences into a distinctive Swahili civilization and language.

keyTerms.def: The 14th-century ruler of the Mali Empire famous for his lavish 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca.
A city in the Songhai Empire renowned as a center of Islamic scholarship, libraries, and education.
A West African empire that succeeded Mali, controlling extensive territory along the Niger River by the 1400s-1500s.
A string of East African trading city-states, such as Kilwa, that connected Africa to Indian Ocean trade networks.

practice.q: The Ghana and Mali Empires built their wealth primarily by
choices: Controlling and taxing trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt
Conquering the Roman Empire
Trading exclusively with China
Mining silver in East Africa
practice.explain: Both Ghana and Mali grew wealthy by controlling key trans-Saharan trade routes that carried gold north and salt south, taxing the merchants who moved these valuable goods across the desert.

practice.q: Timbuktu, under Songhai rule, was especially renowned as
choices: A center of Islamic scholarship with libraries and a university
A coastal trading city on the Indian Ocean
The capital of the Ghana Empire
A center of Christian pilgrimage
practice.explain: Timbuktu became one of the great centers of Islamic learning in the medieval world, hosting large libraries and attracting scholars from across the Muslim world to its university.

practice.q: Swahili coast city-states like Kilwa grew wealthy primarily through
choices: Trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt
Indian Ocean trade in gold, ivory, and other goods reaching Arabia, India, and China
Control of the Mediterranean Sea
Agricultural exports to Europe
practice.explain: Swahili coast cities engaged in extensive Indian Ocean trade, connecting East Africa with merchants from Arabia, India, and China, and blending these influences into a distinctive Swahili culture.

units.title: The Americas and a World on the Verge of Connection
units.summary: While Afro-Eurasia's civilizations grew increasingly interconnected through trade, the Americas developed sophisticated, populous civilizations in complete isolation from the Old World, right up until the eve of a contact that would change both hemispheres forever.

lessons.title: Mesoamerican and Andean Civilizations
lessons.intro: Isolated from Afro-Eurasia by two oceans, the peoples of Mesoamerica and the Andes independently developed writing, mathematics, monumental cities, and vast empires that rivaled anything found in Europe or Asia at the time.

sections.heading: The Maya and Aztec
body: The Maya civilization, flourishing across present-day Mexico and Central America especially between roughly 250 and 900 CE, built independent city-states with impressive pyramid temples, developed one of the most accurate calendar systems in the ancient world, and independently invented the mathematical concept of zero. Maya cities eventually declined for reasons still debated by historians, including drought, warfare, and overpopulation.

Centuries later, the Mexica people, commonly known as the **Aztec**, founded their capital **Tenochtitlan** in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, building it into one of the largest cities in the world by the early 1500s. The Aztec Empire dominated central Mexico through a tribute system that forced conquered peoples to pay regular taxes in goods and labor, and Aztec religion, which included human sacrifice, was central to state ceremony and legitimacy.

sections.heading: The Inca Empire
body: In South America, the **Inca Empire** expanded rapidly in the 1400s to become the largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas, stretching along the Andes Mountains from present-day Colombia to Chile. The Inca built an extensive road system across extremely difficult mountain terrain, connecting their empire's capital, Cusco, to distant provinces and enabling rapid communication via relay runners.

Lacking a traditional writing system, the Inca recorded numerical and administrative information using **quipu**, knotted cords that encoded data through knot type, position, and color. Inca engineers also developed advanced terraced agriculture, carving farmland into steep mountainsides to grow crops like potatoes and maize at high altitudes.

keyTerms.def: The Aztec capital city, founded in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, one of the largest cities in the world by the 1500s.
A highly accurate calendar system developed by the Maya civilization in Mesoamerica.
Knotted cords used by the Inca Empire to record numerical and administrative information without written text.
The largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas, stretching along the Andes Mountains, with its capital at Cusco.

practice.q: How did the Inca Empire record numerical and administrative information without a traditional writing system?
choices: Using hieroglyphics carved in stone
Using quipu, knotted cords that encoded data through knot type, position, and color
Using cuneiform tablets
Using a Maya-style calendar
practice.explain: The Inca used quipu, an intricate system of knotted cords, to record numbers and administrative data, allowing them to manage a vast empire without a conventional writing system.

practice.q: The Aztec capital of Tenochtitlan was built
choices: High in the Andes Mountains
On an island in Lake Texcoco
Along the Nile River
On the coast of the Gulf of Mexico
practice.explain: Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, and by the early 1500s it had grown into one of the largest and most sophisticated cities in the world.

practice.q: What mathematical achievement did the Maya civilization develop independently?
choices: Algebra
The concept of zero
The Hindu-Arabic numeral system
Cuneiform writing
practice.explain: The Maya independently developed the mathematical concept of zero, a significant achievement they reached separately from similar developments in India, and used it within their highly accurate calendar system.

lessons.title: North American Peoples
lessons.intro: North America north of Mexico held no single empire comparable to the Aztec or Inca, but it was far from empty or unorganized: diverse nations built large cities, extensive trade networks, and sophisticated political systems of their own.

sections.heading: Diverse Societies Across a Continent
body: In the arid Southwest, Ancestral Puebloan peoples built remarkable multi-story stone and adobe settlements, including the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, which required sophisticated planning to manage scarce water resources in a challenging desert environment. Around the same period, the **Mississippian culture** built large earthen mound cities along the Mississippi River and its tributaries.

The largest of these, **Cahokia**, located near present-day St. Louis, reached its peak around 1100 CE with a population that may have exceeded 10,000 to 20,000 people, making it, at the time, larger than London. Cahokia's massive Monks Mound and evidence of long-distance trade in copper, shell, and other goods show a society with organized labor, social hierarchy, and extensive regional connections.

sections.heading: Political and Economic Systems
body: In the Northeast, the **Iroquois Confederacy** united several distinct nations under a shared political council that made collective decisions while allowing each member nation significant self-governance, a structure some historians believe later influenced ideas about federalism among early American political thinkers, though the extent of that influence remains debated.

Long before European contact, extensive trade networks connected peoples across the continent, moving goods like copper from the Great Lakes, shells from the Gulf Coast, and obsidian from the Rocky Mountains over vast distances, showing that North American societies, while politically diverse, were far from isolated from one another.

keyTerms.def: The largest Mississippian mound city, near present-day St. Louis, which peaked around 1100 CE.
A Southwestern culture known for multi-story stone and adobe settlements like those at Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde.
A North American culture that built large earthen mound cities along the Mississippi River and its tributaries.
A political alliance of several Native nations in the Northeast governed by a shared council.

practice.q: Cahokia, the largest Mississippian city, is notable because at its peak around 1100 CE it
choices: Was smaller than most European villages
May have had a population larger than London at the time
Was located in the Southwest desert
Was founded by the Aztec Empire
practice.explain: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, reached a population that may have exceeded 10,000 to 20,000 people around 1100 CE, larger than London's population at the time, reflecting a sophisticated, organized society.

practice.q: What structural feature characterized the Iroquois Confederacy?
choices: A single absolute monarch ruling all member nations
A shared council uniting several nations while allowing each significant self-governance
Direct rule by the Aztec Empire
A system based entirely on written law codes
practice.explain: The Iroquois Confederacy united multiple distinct nations under a shared governing council for collective decisions, while each nation retained significant authority over its own internal affairs.

practice.q: Evidence of trade networks across pre-contact North America, such as Great Lakes copper found far from its source, shows that
choices: North American societies were completely isolated from one another
Extensive trade connected diverse peoples across great distances long before European contact
Only coastal peoples engaged in any trade
Trade began only after European arrival
practice.explain: Archaeological evidence of goods like copper, shells, and obsidian traveling vast distances shows that North American peoples maintained extensive trade connections across the continent well before Europeans arrived.

lessons.title: The World in 1500
lessons.intro: By 1500, the Old World's regions were already tightly linked by centuries of trade and technological exchange, and a handful of ambitious European kingdoms were about to turn that existing web of connections into something genuinely global.

sections.heading: A World of Connected Regions
body: By 1500, Afro-Eurasia was already bound together by overlapping trade networks: the Silk Road linked China to Central Asia and the Mediterranean, Indian Ocean trade routes connected East Africa, Arabia, India, and Southeast Asia, and trans-Saharan routes tied West Africa to the Mediterranean world. Along these routes, goods moved alongside ideas and technologies, including papermaking and printing, gunpowder, and the compass, all of which spread gradually westward from Asia over previous centuries.

This existing web of connections meant that by 1500, no major Old World civilization developed in true isolation; ideas, diseases, and trade goods regularly crossed cultural and political boundaries, even without any single power controlling the entire network.

sections.heading: On the Eve of Global Contact
body: Several developments positioned European kingdoms, especially Portugal and Spain, to expand their reach further than ever before. Advances in shipbuilding, particularly the **caravel**, a small, maneuverable ship capable of sailing effectively against the wind, combined with improved navigational tools like the magnetic compass and astrolabe, gave European sailors new capability for long ocean voyages.

At the same time, the **Ottoman Empire**'s control over key eastern Mediterranean and Middle Eastern trade routes, especially after capturing Constantinople in 1453, made established land routes to Asian markets more difficult and costly for European traders, giving Portugal and Spain strong incentive to seek new sea routes to Asia directly, setting the stage for the Age of Exploration that would connect the hemispheres for the first time in human history.

keyTerms.def: A vast pre-modern trade network connecting East Africa, Arabia, India, and Southeast Asia.
A small, maneuverable European sailing ship capable of sailing effectively against the wind, key to long ocean voyages.
A powerful empire that controlled key eastern Mediterranean trade routes after capturing Constantinople in 1453.
The period beginning around 1500 when European powers sought new sea routes to Asia and encountered the Americas.

practice.q: Why is it inaccurate to describe Old World civilizations in 1500 as developing in complete isolation from one another?
choices: Because Europe had already colonized all of Asia by then
Because overlapping trade networks like the Silk Road and Indian Ocean trade routes already connected Africa, Asia, and Europe
Because writing had not yet been invented
Because no trade existed before 1500
practice.explain: By 1500, established networks like the Silk Road, Indian Ocean trade, and trans-Saharan routes already linked Afro-Eurasian civilizations, moving goods, technologies, and ideas across vast distances well before European overseas expansion began.

practice.q: What technological development was especially important in enabling long European ocean voyages by 1500?
choices: The invention of gunpowder
The caravel, combined with the magnetic compass and astrolabe
The printing press
The Great Wall of China
practice.explain: The caravel, a maneuverable ship able to sail effectively against the wind, combined with navigational tools like the compass and astrolabe, gave European sailors the technical capability for sustained long-distance ocean voyages.

practice.q: How did Ottoman control of eastern Mediterranean trade routes after 1453 influence European exploration?
choices: It encouraged Europeans to abandon trade with Asia entirely
It made overland trade routes to Asia more difficult and costly, incentivizing Europeans to seek new sea routes
It had no effect on European trade decisions
It caused Europe to lose all access to Asian goods permanently
practice.explain: Ottoman control over key trade routes following the capture of Constantinople raised the cost and difficulty of overland trade with Asia, giving Portugal and Spain strong incentive to find alternative sea routes, setting the stage for the Age of Exploration.
